title: Guided Practice in Explicit Teaching: The Most Important Part of the Lesson
author: Trudy Mayo
summary: Trudy Mayo argues that guided practice, the We Do phase between modelling and independent work, is the most important and least understood part of an explicit teaching lesson. She says it is defined by what the teacher is doing, namely monitoring, giving feedback and gradually releasing responsibility, rather than by any particular activity such as mini whiteboards or partner talk. Guided practice is also formative assessment in action, because students appear to understand during modelling while the cognitive load sits with the teacher, and gaps surface only once they must think for themselves. She links missing guided practice to off-task behaviour and reteaching during independent work, and lists features of effective practice: immediate feedback, whole-class participation, multiple opportunities to respond, strategic scaffolding and responsive reteaching. The post ends with a pointer to the author's paid resource, but the pedagogical argument stands on its own.
points: Guided practice is defined by the teacher's monitoring, feedback and gradual release rather than by the activity chosen.
Students often seem to understand during modelling because the teacher carries the cognitive load, so guided practice is where misunderstandings first become visible.
Skipping or rushing guided practice often shows up later as off-task behaviour, avoidance and reteaching, which are not necessarily behaviour or motivation problems.
Because it depends on real-time responses to student thinking, guided practice cannot be fully scripted in advance and must be supported by a repertoire of examples and routines.
quotes: Guided practice is where students begin applying new learning while support is still available. It is also where teachers gather the information they need to determine whether learning is actually taking place.

Students often appear to understand during modelling because the cognitive load sits largely with the teacher. Once students are required to complete the thinking themselves, misunderstandings can quickly emerge. Guided practice provides a supported environment where those misunderstandings can be identified and addressed before students move into independent work.

Many teachers think of guided practice as a collection of activities. Whiteboards, partner talk, graphic organisers and collaborative tasks are all common examples. However, guided practice is not defined by the activity being used. It is defined by what the teacher is doing.
These challenges are not always the result of behaviour, motivation or effort. Often, they indicate that students required additional supported practice before being expected to work independently.

Teachers gather responses from every learner rather than relying solely on volunteers (using the mini whiteboards!). Teachers may randomly choose students to share their answers, once all of the boards and responses have been scanned. This provides a more accurate picture of whole-class understanding.

Although teachers can prepare examples, prompts and resources in advance, they cannot fully predict how students will respond. The quality of guided practice depends on the teacher’s ability to respond to student thinking as it unfolds.

As students respond on mini whiteboards, explain their thinking, participate in partner discussions and work through examples together, teachers are continuously gathering information about what students understand and where additional support may be required.
